item.passage:
Aunt Lupe had one rule for the window of the truck, and she had repeated it so often that Rafa could hear it in his sleep: take the order, say it back, then take the money. "The saying back is the part people skip," she told him. "Then they spend the afternoon making food nobody asked for."

On the second Saturday of the market, a little after eleven, she discovered that the tank feeding the grill was running low and that the spare in the back of the truck was empty. The supply store was fifteen minutes away. She looked at the line, which was four people long, and then at Rafa, who was fourteen and had so far been trusted with the cash box and the napkins.

"Twenty minutes," she said, and handed him her apron. "The grill has gas for an hour. Keep the window open." Then she drove off in the white van.

For the first ten minutes he was fast. A woman wanted two chicken tacos and a lemonade; a man in a cycling jersey wanted the bean plate; a family of five wanted things he wrote in a column that ran off the bottom of the order pad. He took the money as soon as each person finished speaking, because the line was growing and speed seemed to be the whole job.

Then the bean plate came back. The man in the jersey had asked for it without cheese, he said politely, and pointed at the cheese. The family's order was short one quesadilla and had an extra horchata that the father said he would drink anyway. A boy of about seven held up a taco and announced that it was the wrong taco. Rafa remade what he could. The line, which had been seven people, was now eleven.

He stood still for a moment with the spatula in his hand. Then he leaned out of the window toward the next customer, a woman with a toddler on her hip, and said, "Tell me again, slowly, and I'll say it back."

She did, and he did: one steak taco, mild, hold the onion, and a cup of rice for the toddler. It took perhaps ten seconds longer than his first way. The order went out right, and so did the next one, and the one after that. Nothing came back to the window. By the time the van pulled into the lot behind the truck, the line was down to three.

Aunt Lupe climbed in, set the new tank by the door, and watched him take one order from start to finish without speaking. Then she asked how it had gone. He told her about the bean plate and the wrong taco, and about the woman with the toddler. When he reached behind his back for the strings of the apron, she shook her head and went to the grill.

The first drops come one at a time,
as if someone on the roof were testing it:
a tack, a pause, a tack,
a seed let fall into an empty pail.

My grandfather sets down his fork and lifts one finger,
the way he does for the radio
when the weather comes on,
and we wait with him.

Then the rest arrives. It does not knock.
It comes down on the tin all at once,
a sound like gravel poured from a truck
that keeps on pouring, and the kitchen
fills with it to the ceiling.

We give up talking. My aunt mouths a word
across the table and laughs when I shake my head.
The dog goes under the stove.
My grandfather picks up his fork again
and eats inside the roar,
content as a man walking his own field.

It is only water. I know that.
The same water falls on the barn, the road,
the pond, the backs of the cows,
and none of them say a thing about it.
The roof is what gives it a voice:
thin metal, bent and nailed,
turning every drop into news.

When it eases, it eases slowly,
gravel to rice, rice to sand,
until the gutter is the loudest thing,
and then the clock, and then my aunt,
finishing the sentence she began
ten minutes ago, as if nothing had happened.

I live now under six floors of concrete.
Rain comes down on the city all night
and I learn of it in the morning
from the dark street and the umbrellas,
the way you hear of something
from a person who was there.

item.passage:
The winter I was thirteen, my grandmother decided I was old enough to split wood. She heated her house with an iron stove that ate an armload every few hours, and her woodpile was a long wall of rounds, sections of trunk sawed to the length of a forearm, stacked under a sheet of plywood beside the porch.

She handed me the maul, which looked like an axe that had been in a fight: a heavy wedge of a head on a hickory handle. I set a round on the chopping block, raised the maul over my head, and brought it down as hard as I could. It bounced. The second time it stuck an inch deep, and I spent several minutes working it loose while my grandmother watched from the porch with her coffee.

"You're hitting it like it owes you money," she said.

She came down the steps, took the maul, and turned the round over twice before she set it on the block. Then she pointed at its top. I saw what she saw only when she traced it with her finger: a thin crack running from the bark toward the center, and another branching off it, like a dry riverbed on a map. "The wood has already decided where it wants to open," she said. "Your job is to agree with it."

She lifted the maul to her shoulder, no higher, and let it fall along the crack. The round came apart in two halves with a sound like a book being shut. She was seventy-one and weighed perhaps a hundred and ten pounds.

For the rest of that winter I read wood. I learned that a knot is a place where a branch once grew, and that the grain twists around it, so a blow aimed at a knot is mostly wasted. I learned that rounds often split more easily on the coldest mornings, when the water inside them had frozen, and that a log that will not open from the top will sometimes open from the bottom. I learned that the swing matters less than the place it lands. By February I could fill the box on the porch before school, and I had stopped coming inside with my shoulders aching.

I heat my own house with wood now, in another state, from a pile I order by the cord. Last fall a neighbor's son came over to help, a strong boy of fifteen. He swung the maul over his head and brought it down on a knot with everything he had. It bounced. He was hitting it, I thought, like it owed him money. I watched him from the porch, holding my coffee, and I waited a little longer than I needed to before I came down the steps.

The winter I was thirteen, my grandmother decided I was old enough to split wood. She heated her house with an iron stove that ate an armload every few hours, and her woodpile was a long wall of rounds, sections of trunk sawed to the length of a forearm, stacked under a sheet of plywood beside the porch.

She handed me the maul, which looked like an axe that had been in a fight: a heavy wedge of a head on a hickory handle. I set a round on the chopping block, raised the maul over my head, and brought it down as hard as I could. It bounced. The second time it stuck an inch deep, and I spent several minutes working it loose while my grandmother watched from the porch with her coffee.

"You're hitting it like it owes you money," she said.

She came down the steps, took the maul, and turned the round over twice before she set it on the block. Then she pointed at its top. I saw what she saw only when she traced it with her finger: a thin crack running from the bark toward the center, and another branching off it, like a dry riverbed on a map. "The wood has already decided where it wants to open," she said. "Your job is to agree with it."

She lifted the maul to her shoulder, no higher, and let it fall along the crack. The round came apart in two halves with a sound like a book being shut. She was seventy-one and weighed perhaps a hundred and ten pounds.

For the rest of that winter I read wood. I learned that a knot is a place where a branch once grew, and that the grain twists around it, so a blow aimed at a knot is mostly wasted. I learned that rounds often split more easily on the coldest mornings, when the water inside them had frozen, and that a log that will not open from the top will sometimes open from the bottom. I learned that the swing matters less than the place it lands. By February I could fill the box on the porch before school, and I had stopped coming inside with my shoulders aching.

I heat my own house with wood now, in another state, from a pile I order by the cord. Last fall a neighbor's son came over to help, a strong boy of fifteen. He swung the maul over his head and brought it down on a knot with everything he had. It bounced. He was hitting it, I thought, like it owed him money. I watched him from the porch, holding my coffee, and I waited a little longer than I needed to before I came down the steps.

A number of rural school districts in the western and midwestern United States have moved to a school week of four days, and the idea now comes up in places far from those first adopters. Its appeal is easy to see. A district that closes its buildings one day a week spends less on buses, heating, and cafeteria staff. A small district competing for teachers can offer something a richer one cannot: every Friday or Monday off. Students, asked about it, tend to vote for it at once.

I think the case deserves a harder look than it usually gets.

Start with the money. The savings sound large because the change sounds large: one day in five, gone. But the buildings still need some heat on the empty day in winter, the teachers are still paid the same salaries, and the remaining four days usually grow longer to make up the hours. Studies of districts that made the switch have generally found the savings to be modest, often a few percent of the budget or less. That is real money for a small district. It is also a good deal less than the change seems to promise.

Then consider learning. A longer school day sounds like an even trade for a shorter week, but an hour added to the end of an afternoon is a poor substitute for a morning, when children are fresh. The research here is mixed. Some studies have found little difference in test scores; several larger ones have found that students in four-day districts gain somewhat less over the years than similar students elsewhere. Mixed evidence is a reason for care, not for confidence.

Finally, there is the fifth day itself. A family with a parent at home, or a grandparent nearby, may find it a gift. A family with two working parents finds a day of child care to arrange and pay for, every week of the school year. Closing a school for a day does not make the day disappear; it hands the day to someone else.

None of this means a four-day week is always wrong. A district that has tried every other way to find teachers may reasonably decide it is the best of the choices in front of it. My question is narrower. Before a district gives away a fifth of its week, it should know what it is getting in return, and it should ask the families who will be holding that day what it will cost them.

In the spring of 1849, a wagon loaded with wheat could take two days to cover the eighteen miles between the farms around Kesterville and the river landing at Port Orrin. The road was dirt, and in March and April it became a trench of mud that held wheels to the hub. Farmers who could wait for summer did. Farmers who could not sold their grain in Kesterville for less.

That year a group of Kesterville merchants formed the Kesterville and Port Orrin Plank Road Company. Their plan, copied from roads already built elsewhere, was simple: lay heavy timbers lengthwise along the route, then nail across them hemlock planks eight feet long and three inches thick, making a wooden floor eighteen miles long. Wagons would pay a toll at each of three gates. The company's engineer, a surveyor named Thomas Eby, estimated that the planks would last ten to twelve years, and the directors used his figure to promise their investors a steady return.

At first the road did everything they had said. A team that had managed a ton on the dirt road could pull two on the planks, and the trip to the landing shrank to a single day in any season. Tolls poured in. For three years the company paid its stockholders more than ten percent a year, paying out nearly every dollar and keeping almost nothing back for the day the planks would wear out.

Eby had measured the planks; he had not measured the ground beneath them. Wood laid on damp earth rots from underneath, out of sight. By the fourth year, wheels were breaking through planks that looked sound from above, and horses were stepping into the holes. The company began replacing planks a few hundred at a time. By the sixth year it was replacing them by the mile, and the toll money that had gone to stockholders was going to sawmills instead.

Then, in 1856, a railroad reached Port Orrin and laid a spur to within three miles of Kesterville. Most of the freight moved to the rails within a season. In 1858 the company sold its gates to the county for less than the cost of a single mile of new planking, and the county pulled up the rotten floor and spread gravel in its place.

Years later, Eby defended his estimate in a letter to the Kesterville paper. Planks of that kind had lasted ten years, he wrote, on roads where they were laid on drained ground and their undersides were tarred. Nobody had asked him to do either, because both cost money, and the money had already been promised.

Their plan, copied from roads already built elsewhere, was simple: lay heavy timbers lengthwise along the route, then nail across them hemlock planks eight feet long and three inches thick, making a wooden floor eighteen miles long. Wagons would pay a toll at each of three gates. The company's engineer, a surveyor named Thomas Eby, estimated that the planks would last ten to twelve years, and the directors used his figure to promise their investors a steady return.

At first the road did everything they had said. A team that had managed a ton on the dirt road could pull two on the planks, and the trip to the landing shrank to a single day in any season.
